newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB money growth target "means to an end" - Gehrig.
newsitem.headline: SNB money growth target "means to an end" - Gehrig.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) board member Bruno Gehrig said on Friday using monetary aggregates to set policy has worked well, but at the same time, sensitivity is needed and the money target should not be an end in itself.
"In the case of monetary disturbances, monetary flexibility is necessary. The monetary growth path is and remains a means to an end, not an end in itself," Gehrig said in the text of a speech.
"It must always leave open room for manoeuver. One should use this (room) in the interest of the overall economy, and avoid over-use." he said.
The SNB is considered by economists to use a strong monetarist orientation in setting policy, in which money supply growth plays a key role.
The SNB has targeted medium-term growth in its monetary base since 1990.

The goal for the current 1995 to end-1999 period is growth of about one percent per year, which is seen as consistent with price stability, defined by Gehrig as a one to two percent rise in the consumer price index per year, although he noted there was no precise answer for the optimal inflation rate. He added the consumer price index tended to exaggerate "real" inflation.
On Friday, the SNB said its central bank money supply rose by an annualised rate of 7.9 percent in February versus the fourth quarter 1996. The growth was 11.4 percent in January.
Gehrig noted that in practice, the growth path has been generously interpreted.

"Demonstrating reliability and credibility with respect to price stability belongs to the art of monetary policy. This can be achieved by sticking to the rules as the 'norm' and responding to a situation as the exception," he said.
SNB data has shown a significant undershooting throughout the early 1990s. The overshooting which began in 1996 continues despite subnormal to negative growth.
The SNB has said previously that it considers factors like exchange rates and employment, in cases of serious disruptions, when formulating its short-term policy.
At the same time, Gehrig said differences between targeting inflation or monetary targets were often exaggerated in theory, but were not that different in practice.
Gehrig noted economist Bennet McCallum had postulated a rule in which the nominal growth or gross domestic product is guided by the production potential.
The more growth came in below target, the higher the growth rate for the monetary basis would be set.
"McCallum's, and our own simulation experiments show that such a rule certainly has its merits," Gehrig said.
"But blind adherence to a policy rule can lead to ruin, that is, to explosive swings in growth," Gehrig said.

Gehrig also noted the popularity of economist John Taylor's formula, especially in the U.S. It calls for a federal funds rate equal to half of the so-called "production gap", plus half of the "inflation gap" plus a "normal" nominal interest rate.
An advantage was that it worked by steering short-term interest rates, which a central bank can directly influence.
"Transfer (of the Taylor formula) to other countries shows, that it would, for example, replicate the monetary policy implemented by the (Swiss) National Bank over large stretches," Gehrig said.
He said the SNB does look at interest rates generated by the Taylor equation and at times uses them as additional information in its assessment of the monetary situation.
He added the same likely holds true for Taylor's as for all other formulas: from simulation to implementation a whole host of "empirical imponderables" must be taken into account.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340.
